books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A: The South grew distinct from the rest of the country. Slavery and cotton came to define Southern society, and white Southerners defended slavery as part of their way of life. Some defenders compared Northern factory workers, who could be fired when business was slow, with enslaved people, who were fed and housed by their owners. Alexis de Tocqueville, visiting in the 1830s, wrote that slavery was the main source of the South's distinctiveness.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A (Southern defense of slavery; Tocqueville on slavery as the main source of Southern distinctiveness).

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A
stem: Most white Southerners owned no slaves, yet most defended slavery. Which reason best explains that support?

options.text: Non-slaveholders were paid by planters to defend slavery in public
options.misconception: Planters did not pay non-slaveholders to defend slavery; the support ran deeper than money.

options.text: Non-slaveholders hoped to sell their farms to Northern factories for a profit
options.misconception: Non-slaveholders farmed their own land; they did not hope to sell to Northern factories.

options.text: White supremacy bound them to slavery, and many hoped to own slaves
Non-slaveholders were barred from voting unless they publicly defended slavery
options.misconception: No law tied voting to defending slavery; white men voted whether or not they owned slaves.

rationales.A: Planters did not pay non-slaveholders to defend slavery. The support ran deeper than money.
rationales.B: Non-slaveholders farmed their own land. They did not hope to sell to Northern factories.
rationales.C: Slavery put every white person above every Black person, and owning slaves was the mark of success, so even those without slaves defended the system.
rationales.D: No law tied voting to defending slavery. White men voted whether or not they owned slaves.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what non-slaveholders gained. Slavery put every white person above every Black person, owner or not.
2. Ask what they hoped. Owning slaves was the mark of success, so many hoped to join the owners one day.
3. Add the fear. Ending slavery would end that rank and that hope, so they defended the system.
Background: Barron's notes that white supremacy, mixed with fear, shaped white Southern views.
Remember: people defend a system that ranks them above others, even when they own little of it.
